answer_text:
Assume the standard Fourier-transform convention

\[
g(w)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)e^{-iwx}\,dx .
\]

If \(f\) has a finite second moment, i.e. \(x^2 f(x)\in L^1(\mathbb R)\), then we may differentiate under the integral sign:

\[
g''(w)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (-ix)^2 f(x)e^{-iwx}\,dx
      =-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 f(x)e^{-iwx}\,dx .
\]

Evaluating at \(w=0\),

\[
g''(0)=-\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 f(x)\,dx .
\]

So the desired integral is determined by the curvature of \(g\) at the origin.

Now, if the statement

\[
g(w)\approx 1-w^2 \qquad (w\ll 1)
\]

means that this is the second-order Taylor behavior, i.e.

\[
g(w)=1-w^2+o(w^2)\quad\text{as }w\to 0,
\]

then

\[
g''(0)=-2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2 f(x)\,dx=-g''(0)=2.
\]

The full range of \(g(w)\) is not needed for this particular moment; only the local quadratic coefficient at \(w=0\) matters. However, if “approximately” is only a qualitative statement and does not fix the exact \(w^2\) coefficient, then the exact value is not determined.

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes, if }g(w)=1-w^2+o(w^2)\text{ at }w=0;\text{ then the integral is }2.\text{ Otherwise, not uniquely.}}
\]
